sections.h2: How are Virginia's cities and counties organized?
sections.html:
Virginia has two kinds of local governments that matter to a house seller: counties and independent cities. Since 1871, every municipality incorporated as a city in Virginia has been an independent city, and none of the 38 is politically part of a county.

That setup is unusual. Of the 41 independent cities in the United States, 38 are in Virginia, and the other three are Baltimore, St. Louis and Carson City. The Census Bureau treats them as county equivalents, which is why a city like Richmond or Norfolk is handled as its own jurisdiction instead of as part of a county.

Towns work differently. A Virginia town always sits inside a county, has limited powers set by its charter and usually shares courts and the public school division with that county. If your house is inside a town, ask the treasurer which governments bill it.

Some cities are completely surrounded by one county and form enclaves. Twelve independent cities also serve as the seat of the county around them, including Charlottesville, Fairfax, Harrisonburg, Manassas, Salem, Staunton, Williamsburg and Winchester.

sections.h2: Why does the city versus county line matter when you sell?
sections.html:
It helps decide which local offices and courts you deal with, because a city stands on its own while a county and the towns inside it share courts and many services.

  • Courts: a first-class city such as Richmond has its own district court and its own circuit court.
  • A second-class city has its own district court but no circuit court of its own, so the City of Fairfax shares a circuit court with Fairfax County and Falls Church shares one with Arlington County.
  • Assessments: the commissioner of the revenue or another local assessing officer sets the value in the county or city.
  • Appeals: a board of equalization in the county or city hears complaints about assessments.

In practice, when a deed or a lawsuit is involved, the first step is learning whether the property sits in a city or a county.

sections.h2: Which Virginia cities have changed over time?
sections.html:
Several independent cities in the Hampton Roads and Richmond regions came from mergers, and a few gave up city status. The history explains why some modern city boundaries look odd on a map.

CityWhat happened
HamptonMerged with Elizabeth City County and the Town of Phoebus in 1952
Newport NewsWarwick, formed in 1952, consolidated into an expanded Newport News in 1958
ChesapeakeFormed in 1963 when South Norfolk merged with Norfolk County
SuffolkCombined with the short-lived city of Nansemond in 1974
RichmondAbsorbed Manchester by agreement in 1910
BedfordGave up its city charter in 2013 and is now a town in Bedford County

If a property record or an old deed refers to a name that no longer exists, ask the local clerk which jurisdiction holds the land records today.

sections.h2: What does it cost to record a deed in Virginia?
sections.html:
Two state taxes apply when a deed is recorded, and one of them is usually paid by the seller. They are in 58.1-801 and 58.1-802.

  • The state recordation tax is 25 cents on every $100, or fraction of $100, of the greater of the deed's consideration or the property's actual value.
  • For that purpose, value means the most recent property tax assessment at the time of conveyance.
  • A separate grantor tax is 50 cents for each $500, or fraction, of the consideration or value when it is above $100, not counting liens that remain on the property.
  • The grantor, meaning the seller, pays the grantor tax, but the two sides may agree that the buyer pays some or all of it.
  • The consideration must appear on the first page of the document, and the clerk certifies that the tax was paid before the deed is recorded.

As an illustration only, a $300,000 sale works out to about $750 of state recordation tax and $300 of grantor tax using those rates. Localities may add their own recordation tax under a separate section, and half of the grantor tax goes to the state and half to the locality. Your title company or the clerk can give an exact total for your closing.

sections.h2: How is property tax assessed and appealed across Virginia?
sections.html:
Each locality assesses its own real estate, and an owner who disagrees can go to a local board of equalization. The statute, 58.1-3379, tells the board to treat the assessor's value as correct unless the taxpayer shows otherwise.

  • The owner must show by a preponderance of the evidence that the property is valued above fair market value, or that the assessment is not uniform and not based on accepted appraisal practice.
  • For a home with fewer than four residential units, the assessor must give records on request within 15 days.
  • If the assessor does not, the assessor presents its records and testimony before the taxpayer does.
  • The board may consider market sales through December 31 before the effective date of the assessment, if submitted by the locality's deadline.
  • The board may raise assessments as well as lower them, to even out the tax burden.

Filing deadlines and hearing dates differ by locality, so we have left them out. Ask your commissioner of the revenue or assessor for the current calendar.

sections.h2: What tax relief programs exist for Virginia homeowners?
sections.html:
The state lets localities set up relief for older and disabled homeowners and requires one exemption for severely disabled veterans. The rules differ from one county or city to the next.

Under 58.1-3210, a governing body may by ordinance exempt or defer real estate tax on the sole dwelling of an owner who is at least 65 or, if the ordinance includes it, permanently and totally disabled. Under 58.1-3219.5, a veteran rated 100 percent service-connected, permanent and total disabled is exempt on the principal residence and up to one acre of land for tax years from 2011, and a surviving spouse keeps the exemption until remarriage.

If you inherit a house or sell one that was under a deferral, ask the treasurer whether deferred taxes come due at transfer.

sections.h2: What creditor protection does a Virginia homeowner have?
sections.html:
Virginia's homestead exemption protects up to $50,000 in value of a principal residence from creditor process, plus $5,000 of any property ($10,000 at 65 or older) and $500 per dependent, under Va. Code 34-4.

It must be claimed by a recorded deed, it does not apply against purchase-price debts or support obligations, and the dollar amounts are to be adjusted for inflation starting April 1, 2027. A fuller explanation is on our homestead exemption guide.

sections.h2: What do sellers face most often in Virginia?
sections.html:
Most Virginia sellers deal with the same handful of local steps, whether the house is in a city or a county.

  • Finding the right office, which starts with knowing whether the house is in an independent city or in a county.
  • Paying the transfer taxes above and getting the consideration on the face of the deed.
  • Checking the tax bill and any relief or deferral on the property.
  • Dealing with tenants, since evictions are handled in the general district court under state law.
  • Clearing creditors or heirs before the sale can close.

We buy houses in Virginia as they sit and can talk through any of these.

faqs.q: How many independent cities does Virginia have?
faqs.a: Thirty-eight. Virginia has more independent cities than any other state, and none of them is part of a county. Twelve of them also serve as county seats.

faqs.q: Do I pay recordation tax when I sell a house in Virginia?
faqs.a: The state recordation tax applies to the deed, and the grantor tax of 50 cents per $500 is paid by the seller unless the parties agree the buyer pays. Ask your title company for the total, because localities may add their own tax.

faqs.q: What counts as the value for Virginia recordation tax?
faqs.a: The greater of the deed's consideration or the property's value, and value means the most recent property tax assessment at the time of conveyance.

faqs.q: Who hears a property tax appeal in Virginia?
faqs.a: A local board of equalization in the county or city. It presumes the assessor's value is correct, so the owner must present evidence of overvaluation or non-uniformity.

faqs.q: Can a Virginia town and county both tax my house?
faqs.a: A town always lies within a county and shares many services with it. Ask the treasurer which governments bill a house inside town limits.

faqs.q: Is there a state tax exemption for disabled veterans in Virginia?
faqs.a: Yes. A veteran rated 100 percent service-connected, permanent and total disabled is exempt on the principal residence and up to one acre of land, and a surviving spouse keeps it until remarriage.
